A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same source-screening research, with matching core algorithms, experiments and theoretical results. Both versions, including their appendices, are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic subspace-estimation experiments in Figures 1–4 and ACSIncome/CelebA classification results in Table 2.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds neural-network and reweighting results on ACSIncome in Tables 4–5.

M1.justification: The proposed screening Algorithms 1–2 retain their selection, factorization and pruning procedures. Section 5 reuses the screening framework through effective local heads. Appendix D introduces downstream learner tests and reweighting comparators without replacing the proposed screening method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate clustered and heterogeneous-Gaussian synthetic regression, ACSIncome income classification and CelebA smile classification. The added ACSIncome experiments change learner configurations and aggregation strategies, without introducing a new dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: Appendix D.6 adds two evaluated reweighting comparators: inverse-factor weighting and inverse-factor weighting combined with source data volume. The original estimator and screening comparisons are retained; Table 4 reuses the existing full-population, random-selection and power-of-choice baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix D.5 adds ACSIncome configurations using two-layer ReLU networks with hidden dimensions 64 and 256 under FedRep. These supplement the retained logistic-regression experiment. Existing synthetic settings and CelebA preprocessing are preserved, with much of their description moved to Appendix D.

E4.justification: Appendices D.5–D.6 add focused ACSIncome analyses testing screening with nonlinear feature extractors and whether reweighting all sources can substitute for removing sources. The existing dimensionality, population-size and imbalance sensitivity studies remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 5 newly identifies and reports standard deviations for classification accuracy, making variability in the reweighting comparison explicit. Both versions already specify averaging over 20 random seeds and display synthetic error bars; no increase in run count is established.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 values and Figures 1–4 findings are retained. New Table 4 reports screening accuracies of 80.13% and 79.96% at hidden dimensions 64 and 256, versus 79.91% and 79.49% for full-population training. Table 5 adds reweighting results of 79.38% and 79.58%, below subsampling's 79.96%. These are additional ACSIncome configurations.

T1.justification: New Section 5 and Appendix C extend the analysis to nonlinear source-specific response functions over a shared linear projection. They introduce effective heads defined by E[h_i(U)U], Gaussian-covariate and regularity assumptions, and an argument transferring admissibility and minimax rates to this setting. The original linear proofs are largely retained.

C1.justification: v3's abstract, introduction and contribution list explicitly add a theoretical extension of source screening to nonlinear models. v1's theoretical contribution is framed around linear subspace learning, although it already reports nonlinear empirical applications. The central claim that screening can retain minimax optimality remains.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies that the optimality argument can use other estimators that are minimax optimal under well-conditioned settings. Appendix D.6 newly discusses obstacles to extending the guarantees to reweighting and interprets its lower variability but lower mean accuracy relative to subsampling.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the ReLU architecture and hidden dimensions for the added ACSIncome experiments and gives the exact aggregation formulas for both reweighting variants. Most synthetic-generation, dataset-partitioning and ViT preprocessing details in Appendix D were already documented in v1's main text.

R1.justification: The bibliography, related-work survey and prior-rate comparisons retain the same works and research positioning. The nonlinear extension builds on Niu et al. (2024), whose nonlinear results were already acknowledged in v1.

P1.justification: v3 substantially revises the abstract, introduction and problem exposition, adds a section roadmap and an algorithm walkthrough, and standardizes source/client terminology. It also reorganizes experimental exposition by moving detailed settings into Appendix D and incorporating the nonlinear extension into the main narrative.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn with larger labels and revised legend presentation, including changed color assignments in Figure 2. Table 1 is restyled, and Tables 4–5 are added. Figures 3–4 retain the same graphics, and the overall document layout remains similar.

improvement.justification: v3 makes the nonlinear extension's assumptions explicit and tests meaningful questions about nonlinear learners and reweighting, including accuracy variability. Clearer exposition and redrawn figures also improve assessability. These are useful but focused gains: the additional empirical evidence is confined to ACSIncome, and the nonlinear-response theory still assumes a shared linear projection.
